sections.html: Butler County is in southwestern Ohio. Hamilton is both the seat and the biggest city. The 2020 census counted 390,357 residents, and the July 2025 estimate is 400,128. Owners occupy 69.9 percent of the 146,822 households, the typical owner-occupied home is valued at $258,500, and median household income is $81,590. Sixteen school districts, including Lakota, Fairfield, Hamilton, Middletown and Talawanda, reach into the county, which means your bill turns on the taxing districts your parcel sits in.

The auditor reports a median residential and agricultural increase of 19 percent for tax year 2026, payable in 2027, and a median 20 percent for commercial and industrial property. The auditor's sales ratio sits near 90 percent of full market value. Increases vary a lot by place.

Voted levies can move a bill more than value does. A new countywide 2-mill developmental disabilities levy runs about $70 per $100,000 of value, and a 4.49-mill Fairfield Township fire levy runs about $157 per $100,000. New state laws soften the effect of higher values, and second-half bills carry an inflation cap credit under House Bill 186.

Ohio reappraises every six years and updates values at the three-year midpoint. In Butler County 2026 is the latest reappraisal, updates came in 2023 and come again in 2029, and the next reappraisal is 2032.

sections.h2: How the tax bill is figured
sections.html:
Start with the auditor's fair market value and take 35 percent of it. That is the taxable value. Multiply by the combined mill rate, divide by 1,000, then add levies and special assessments and subtract any reduction credits.

  • Parcel numbers. A real estate parcel is a letter followed by 13 numbers, and about 160,000 parcels exist in the county.
  • Taxing districts. The treasurer counts 66 separate districts, so a house in Hamilton and one in Liberty Township can carry different rates.
  • Reduction factors. A levy cannot raise more than it did when voters passed it, so the state applies a reduction factor to the gross rate.
  • Credits. The non-business credit and the owner-occupancy credit apply only to levies in place before the November 2013 election. Homestead is a separate reduction for qualifying seniors and disabled owners.

Special assessments for street paving or weed removal also show on the bill and go back to the government that levied them.

The treasurer collects twice a year. The first half is typically due in mid to late February and the second half in early August, and the printed bill carries the exact date. If a bill never arrives, call the treasurer at (513) 887-3181.

Because Ohio bills in arrears, a payment made in 2026 covers tax year 2025. Section 323.121 sets the late charge: 5 percent when full payment lands within the first ten days after the due date, and 10 percent after that.

Interest is added twice a year. On older balances it starts the first of the month after the second-half due date, and a second charge lands December 1 on everything still unpaid. An owner can file an Application for Remission of Penalty, but the law allows remission only in limited cases.

A complaint about value goes to the Board of Revision. Three people sit on it: the auditor, the treasurer and one county commissioner. It looks at value only, never at how much tax you owe. The filing window is January 1 to March 31, and an owner generally files once in each three-year valuation period.

  • Fill out DTE Form 1, Complaint Against the Valuation of Real Property, and attach your evidence of value.
  • Submit it through the office's online vendor, by email to bor@bcohio.gov, or by mail.
  • A Notice of Hearing arrives by email or certified mail.
  • Allow three to four weeks after the hearing for the Notice of Result.

A request to cut market value by $50,000 or more can draw a counter-complaint from another eligible party such as a school board. After a decision, the owner has 30 days from the mailing date to appeal to the Ohio Board of Tax Appeals or the county Court of Common Pleas, and must notify the board of revision as well.

sections.h2: What sellers pay at the auditor and recorder
sections.html:
Every deed stops at the auditor before it reaches the recorder. The auditor's conveyance fee is a conveyance fee of $3.00 per thousand of the price, with the price rounded up to the next hundred, plus $.50 for each parcel. Real estate has a $3.00 minimum plus the parcel fee. The auditor takes cash, or a check payable to the Butler County Auditor.

DTE Form 100 goes with an ordinary sale and Form 100EX with an exempt transfer. Attach the legal description, and have the Engineer's Office at 513-867-5744 preapprove it before you submit. Transfers can come by mail, in person or by e-file.

The recorder's fee sheet, effective January 1, 2025, lists these charges:

  • $39.00 for a deed, mortgage or lease up to two pages, including a $5.00 preservation surcharge, and $8.00 per added page.
  • $20.00 more for a document that misses the standard layout rules.
  • $4.00 per reference for a satisfaction or release.
  • $2.00 per page for copies and $1.00 per document to certify.

Put a parcel number on each deed and include a self-addressed stamped return envelope, plus a prepared-by statement when the notary is in Ohio. Turnaround is 24 hours. The recorder's office is at 130 High Street in Hamilton, phone (513) 887-3192.

If a bill is still open when you sell, the balance gets settled at closing. Have the title company request a payoff figure from the treasurer, and expect unpaid tax, penalty and interest to come out of your proceeds. A cash buyer can close on a short timeline with the same payoff process and skips the wait for lender appraisal and underwriting. Whoever handles the closing should confirm what is owed on the second half before the deed goes to the auditor.

faqs.q: When is the second-half Butler County tax bill due?
faqs.a: It is usually due in early August, and the first half in mid to late February. The printed bill carries the exact date.

faqs.q: How did Butler County values change in 2026?
faqs.a: Residential and agricultural values rose by a median of 19 percent, and commercial and industrial by 20 percent. Changes differ by place, from a median 39 percent in Lemon Township to 12 percent in the city of Fairfield. New voted levies affect the bill as much as value does.

faqs.q: Can I appeal my Butler County valuation every year?
faqs.a: Generally no. An owner may file once in each three-year valuation period, with some exceptions the statute lists. The window runs January 1 to March 31, and DTE Form 1 is the form to use.

faqs.q: What conveyance fee applies to a Butler County sale?
faqs.a: The auditor charges $3.00 per thousand of the price (rounded up to the next hundred) and $.50 per parcel. Checks go to the Butler County Auditor. Call the auditor at 513-887-3154 about exemptions that call for Form 100EX.

faqs.q: What will the Butler County Recorder charge for a deed?
faqs.a: A deed up to two pages is $39.00 with the $5.00 preservation surcharge built in, and each extra page is $8.00. A document that fails the layout standard adds $20.00. Call (513) 887-3192 with questions.
